utterances.text: I don't know when he left. Since he saw I was ill -- he actually called me to check out the operative documents at the level of the brigade. When he saw that I was really sick, that I was perspiring, that I had a fever, he told me to go home and to do whatever I could to get better, and that it wasn't that urgent, that I could check these documents out in the morning. So I went home, and I don't know when Mr. Cerkez left headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you go back to the brigade, to the brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned earlier in the morning. I wanted to check out these documents. And since the men on duty were doing their jobs, I came to headquarters early in the morning. Perhaps it was 5.30. I can't say for sure now. At any rate, before official working hours, that is to say, before 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the evening, after you found out about this from Cerkez, did you discuss this with your colleagues? Did you discuss this information that you received from Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received this information from Mr. Cerkez, I spent five or ten minutes, at the most, in headquarters and I talked to a few colleagues. And they said, "What is this?" And one of them said, "Well, this is the usual thing, provocations as usual. Well, nothing particular. Perhaps we should be more alert at the front line and perhaps a few people should be sent to the route towards Kruscica." So nothing special. I turned around and went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went home, what were your personal thoughts about this? What was your conclusion on the basis of everything that you had heard? What was your perception?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is how I took it. Until then, on several occasions there were some minor incidents, when the Operative Zone also told us in writing that we should be on the alert, that we should increase the level of combat readiness. That simply meant that a few men should go to certain positions and that they should be ready to act in a more operative fashion. As for calling up other personnel from home or if there was a group that was together, well, perhaps -- well, that's it: keeping that level of alertness. I thought that that was it, and I assumed that perhaps the situation was a bit more serious because of the events that had occurred recently, like what happened to Mr. Totic and all that. That's well-known. But I don't know. Not in my wildest dreams did I believe that there would have been an open conflict. I don't know. This was simply inconceivable to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, that evening there was also some information about Kuber.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, while I was still at headquarters -- well, I don't know whether it was the officer on duty who received this information or whether somebody had come from the outside and said that he had heard some kind of shooting from the direction of Kuber, but we did not have any special information. Later on I found out that through communications, wire communications - I think it was wire communications - they were trying to check what was going on up there, but they didn't succeed. Only later, a day or two later, I found out that up there there was shooting, that there were casualties. I think that two of our members went missing that day and they are still registered as missing. That's what I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for a full understanding, and in relation to maps presented by Witness Elford, I would like that the witness show us a map of the position which was described as a main position for the brigade, where they should expect a possible attack, simply for better understanding, so we all have the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can be referred to any exhibit, if it's an exhibit. Or if you want to put a map in, do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to put the map, this graphically good map, where the points are clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look at it. If you're going to put this in, you'll have to explain who has marked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will explain everything, Your Honour, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have an Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D85/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Sajevic, is it correct that you prepared this map and that you explained the positions to me through this map?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court, starting from the legend, what it says, and briefly what these lines mean and what you are trying to depict.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to depict on this map the positions of the personnel of the Viteska Brigade on the 16th of April at 0530 hours. Later, I was familiarised with the document received from the Operative Zone, ordering the takeover of these positions, as mentioned, at 0530 hours in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the registry to get document D60/2 for us so that we can ask the witness whether that is the order that he has just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While that's being done, does this map show the positions after the forces had moved into the places they were ordered to, or does it show before?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in the legend it says, and that is how I wanted to show it, that this was the situation, the deployment, at half past 5.00 in the morning, based on the order received. So that is where our forces were to be at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Sajevic, I shall now ask you to look at this order. This is a document already adduced. From its contents, can you tell us if it is these positions that were referred to a few hours before that by Cerkez? Is that what he told you, that he had received a verbal order and that it would arrive in writing in due time? Would that be it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these positions which you drew here on the map are showing the positions requested in item 1 of the order?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the order, that is, item 1 of the order, lays down the task for the brigade? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is what you drew here?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention to item 3 of the order, where Commander Blaskic gives a description, and I shall read it now: "In front of you are the forces of the 4th Battalion of the military police. Behind you are your forces. To the right of you are the forces of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski unit, and to the left of you are the civilian forces." Now, in view of this description, from which angle is it, was it viewed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is from the south northward, that is, towards Zenica, from which one expected that possible sabotage and subversion groups might be infiltrating. So it was in that direction, from that point of view. So it is northward, from the south. So the first thing, to avoid any confusion, or rather south-west to north-east. That is the direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Superior Commander writes this order looking in the direction of the strongest enemy forces from which he expects an attack? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we reconstruct it on this map, then, and if this item 3 is projected, superimposed on this map, what does it mean? If you are somewhere here on the river, on the blue line, where then is the 4th Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this definition, the Military Police 4th Battalion is to the north-east, from our position, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, it is between you and Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do we have any closer identification, what is to the north-east? What do you have in the north-east?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What localities are there, because we have indicated the enemy positions here. What localities did the 4th Military Police Battalion hold?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in any event, in front of the forward positions of the BH army, I wouldn't know the exact localities because, I mean, I wasn't there. I didn't make a round of those places at that time. But -- so -- but naturally, they would be -- let me simplify it that they were between these two green lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you use the pointer to show it to us on this map.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it would be logical for them to be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that they could also be in the territory of Ahmici and villages around Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does this mean, "behind you are your forces"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are looking -- may I just explain something, if I may? To me, this order is slightly contradictory because at some -- it says, "Forces behind you. Forces in front." In both cases, the positions of the Vitez Brigade men are clearly defined. But if we look at item three, which says that the forces of the 4th Battalion are in front of us, then evidently, it is the direction Vitez/Zenica which is meant. In that case, the forces which are behind us are merely groups of 15 to 20 strong which was in the motel in Kruscica. Those men -- those forces could then be behind us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the motel where the departures of your shifts to Kamenjas, Slatka Vode were prepared; is that the group that you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean, "to the left of you are civilian police forces"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Might that be -- what would you say -- "to the left of us" means civilian police forces, those would be the forces practically in the town itself, and facing those BH army forces which were in Mahalla, in Stari Vitez. So that would be to the left of us. If we look at item two -- no, item three, excuse me, so that would be to the left of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the right of you, Nikola Subic-Zrinjski, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that our right neighbour was the HVO brigade from Busovaca, then to the right of us were men of the Busovaca HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And not far from your right flank is also the municipal boundary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that means then that Nikola Subic-Zrinjski was in the territory of its municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This need not be the municipal boundary taken literally?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Plus/minus 100 metres does not really mean anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third thing that I wanted us to ascertain from this order is as follows: Could you explain item two, please, briefly? What does that mean? Because it defines in detail, it lays out in detail the task for your troops, four your brigade. So one is the direction and two is the particulars. Could you tell us, what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item two to me, it simply complied with the layout of orders, that is, this is where tasks for smaller groups are set out. So you have the assignments so that one could know what group is tasked with what. But to me, to my mind, this one combat assignment was not necessary because I gathered that this was to mean rather the blocking of communications to prevent access from Kruscica into town for some forces of the BH army. And these forces here, I don't really know. Perhaps up there Vrasnjska, Crveno Brdce, which is the wooded area and their forces could be used to search the woods to see if, perchance, some groups were infiltrated there or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the final question about this order: Does it transpire from any of the components of this order that your unit had been ordered an offensive active operation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If one looks at some categorisation of military orders, is this a offensive or a defensive order?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is evidently a defensive order, and that is what its title says too. But even the order itself shows that this is a form of combat operation of a purely defensive nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are moving from the map. If you want us to take it into consideration, Mr. Kovacic, it's not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I do that for tomorrow? We simply omitted that. It is one sentence. I, of course, will read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The text on the map is -- first title is "Polodzaj" which means position. Then there is the text "Dijelava Viteska Brigade" [Interpretation], parts of the Vitez Brigade, 16th of April 1993 at 5.30. And then in brackets, in red, "zap" which is an abbreviation for order. "OZZP," which is Operative Zone or military district. SB of Central Bosnia, of 16th of April 1993 at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is D62, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And at the top, it also has and it is D60/2 and we have the time, the date, 16th of April half past 1.00. So this was in the early hours of the morning of the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the witness can explain the map. First of all, what is does "VBR" mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know really. There was no room here to write "Vitez Brigade". "ZP" means the command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Command post, thank you. What is "STO Vitez"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- this is the sign for the command post of the Territorial Defence staff of Vitez which was in Mahalla, this was the Bosniak Territorial Defence staff or headquarters in the Bosniak part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. "ZP Vitez", what is that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command post of the military district of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The green lines, what do they represent?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The green lines on this map represent an imagined line separating the territory which is, conditionally speaking, is controlled by the HVO, that is the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is from the upper green line northward, all of that up there was controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; villages equally as roads and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the picture. And the blue line, what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the blue line represents the positions of some parts of the Vitez Brigade on the 16th of April at half past 5.00 when the -- that was the hour when the forces were ordered to be prepared in case of -- if it transpired that it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that we have this fully, we can see a "325. " Is that referring to a Muslim Brigade, do we take that to be?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was the command post of the 325th Mountain Brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And beneath that a circle, what is the blue circle beneath that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This blue circle represents a point of fact our man who was at the Plava Motel in Kruscica, and they were about 15 to 20 men strong I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, we should also notice the triangle flag on the north side marked number "2".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, will you please tell us what does this triangle 2 next to Preocica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means the command post of the battalion, that is the 2nd Battalion of the 325th Brigade had its command post in Preocica which was seen 2/325, that is the military marking. This was the 2nd Battalion of the 325th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the to the south-east, the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 1st Battalion is in the south, in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps to avoid any doubts because I'm not quite sure that everything is clear, the blue line to the south represents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. [In English] We can leave the map in case anybody would like to put some question on it. We can remove it. [Interpretation] And in the morning, what happened in the morning? Was there an attack or wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, as I told you, I came to the Command, to the headquarters, rather early. I went through the operations log book because we did not have any war journal, war log book, although one does do that in wartime but we didn't simply keep that. I don't know why. Perhaps there was no intensive operations and there wasn't such a practice to note down everything that happened on a daily basis. But be that as it may, in the morning, I don't know at what time, around 6.00, one could hear some exchange of fire and at first, it did not sound out of the ordinary because one could hear shots fired around Vitez and around -- because people would get drunk and then would fire off. So that it -- the intensity of that fire was not such that one would think that it might grow into a major conflict, and it was only when shells began to fall over Vitez that one began to realise that the matter was serious. But I'd like to mention once again that at that time, I was still ill. I was still running a high fever. So that Mr. Cerkez, when he arrived at the headquarters, because he was not there when I came, after half an hour or so, he again sent me back home or rather sent me to a doctor. And I went to see the doctor on the 16th in the morning, that is, I went to the emergency unit and they gave me some injections and administered some medicines and the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So that hour and a half or perhaps two that you say you spent there at the headquarters, did you get any reliable information, any verified information about the situation in the municipality during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No reliable, no trustworthy information reached us at that time, at least I didn't know what was going on. We assumed that at Kuber there was something because the day before we learned that the -- that there was some firing exchanged up there. So even though I wasn't there that day, that information arrived that our men were killed at Kuber. At Kuber, we subsequently turned out that two of our men were missing and they were not coming back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you told us that Cerkez came. Did Cerkez bring along some more information, perhaps, with him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not -- he was not any better informed. And then I -- and I think he said that that slight exchange of fire perhaps made him hurry to work. And that at least in those parts where parts of the -- of the segments where the Vitez Brigade parts were positioned, no attempts had been made for a breakthrough by the BH army from Kruscica but we had to -- but they had to stay there until the order was modified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get a picture through all of that which meant that nothing was -- nothing of importance was happening in that area where he was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the picture I got, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like the usher to have this document handed out, please. Please, these are copies of the registry book in the medical centre. Well, it is a double-faced page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last page when you receive a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not translated again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will explain what that is, just merely as a confirmation. This document, we have for a long time. It was produced by my investigator, who copied this book, because we presumed that there might be some relevant information, some checking from time to time. And when the witness, after coming in The Hague, told us that he was sick, we checked that protocol and we found him on the page related to April 16. So perhaps we can ask the witness what medicine was prescribed, because that is the only document from some of that information, and I guess that is international.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you the document, the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I saw it by my own eyes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. But do you have it here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- eighteen months before in the health centre in Vitez. But no, not here, not at this time. I'm trying to tell you that we really copied it at that time for our purposes when we are trying to find some person to establish it, and I merely use the opportunity to check whether a visit of this witness was recorded or not. Perhaps I can ask him for the medicine he got and then we'll see the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to be over-technical, but it's pretty obvious the range of objections I could take if I wanted to. I don't want to take time on it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If that is considered as any serious evidence, I can bring a book in a couple of weeks from Vitez, but I don't know whether the institution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but don't put in untranslated documents. We've now have two running. You know what the rules are, Mr. Kovacic. Yes, we can read. "Penicillin," it says. Is that right, Major: You received some penicillin?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I don't think we should put the document in for the moment. I think it's pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was merely for information, Your Honour. I don't think that really could be evidence. But if needed, we can bring the book from -- the original protocol from the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- or some authorised copy, because I don't know whether they will be able to give it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Sajevic, when did you return, then, to the headquarters, that is?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to headquarters, I think it was the 17th, for a short period of time. And then I went again to get these injections and medicines and I was receiving injections for five or six days. I'm not sure, but I think that already on the 18th -- from the 18th onwards, I was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. At that moment when you came, what was the basic activity going on in headquarters, as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I found chaos, to put it mildly, at headquarters. Because I saw people being brought in from Vitez, people I knew, Bosniaks, military-age men. I saw -- since there was shelling in Vitez, I think that headquarters moved from upstairs to downstairs, I mean just one storey down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, perhaps I did not put a very precise question. I'm not talking about the building. We'll get back to that later. But what was the activity of headquarters concentrated on? What was their main activity?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main activity was increased requests for reinforcement of the Viteska Brigade. They were looking for men because there was an enhancement of combat operations in the wider territory of the municipality. I'm trying to say that the lines of confrontation were expanded, reinforcements were necessary, and personnel had to be provided for these activities. At that time, we still had a shift at Slatka Vode, those we were sending regularly. I think that there were problems at the time. People could not come back from up there, from Slatka Vode, because they had to pass through some Muslim villages in Novi Travnik. Since there had been provocations before that and buses with our men were stoned, we were afraid to send them; we were afraid to withdraw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me, please: At that moment, you said the 18th or two days after the conflict started, mobilisation was already declared or not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think mobilisation was declared in a way, but you could not do it through classical means, through the mass media, because I think that there had been no electricity in quite a few places. Also you could not send classical call-up papers to conscripts, because I believe that these call-up papers had not been prepared and also the courier service did not work. There was no one to distribute this. So there were some activists who worked on the set-up of shifts before that. They were supposed to look for personnel and to look for all of those who had already participated in certain actions, and they were to ask them to report at certain positions. That's the way it went. There was not an organised system of carrying out mobilisation, nor could there have been one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, mobilisation did start, as it could?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only it -- well, it went the way it could have gone, by all the means we had available to us then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Sajevic: Was there any difference -- no. This question is too complicated. Did military conscripts who lived in town report for this mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hardly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A certain number certainly did report?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, a small number, but not as many as we had expected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a general idea in terms of what your estimate was and what actually happened? I know that you don't have the exact date, but --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say it was about 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These 30 per cent, where were they sent? To which locations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were sent to our defence lines that were still being established; that is to say that some were sent to Kuber, Krtina-Mahala, Bobasi, those lines, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were positions reinforced around Vranjska, Crveno Brdce, specifically?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And positions vis-à-vis Kruscica, were they reinforced?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please: The mobilisation response of military conscripts living in villages, military-age men in villages, how did they respond to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. At that time, throughout the municipality, that is to say, in that part that was under HVO control, there was general chaos. One could not expect members of the Viteska Brigade who were at their homes, naturally, because we never had the 300 men we mentioned all together in one place, nor could we have kept them that way. That is to say, that once their shift was over, these men went home. However, no one could expect these men to leave their homes, their families, their wives, their children, their parents. And there was shooting around their houses. Do you understand what I'm saying? So although at that time they were probably aware of the fact that something big was going on, they stayed at home, defending their own homes, their own villages, hamlets. So this response to mobilisation, well, one can say for sure that it was poor here, but then on the other hand, it was good in a way. But these people stayed in their own villages, and only later all of this had to be brought together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the response that you mentioned in percentage points for the urban areas was better than that that you had in the rural areas?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to say now, in terms of percentage particularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There's another question that stems from this. At Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that moment, during these first days of the war -- and it is very difficult to make a distance between one day, two days, three days -- in the Viteska Brigade, your junior officers, could you send a soldier from village A to village B, for example?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hardly. With great difficulty. I already mentioned that from every village there was a group of younger men who went on operations towards Vlasic, Jajce. However, when this real shooting began, then the elderly men also joined in, who were sometimes in these village guards, securing their village during the night. However, it was very difficult to move people from one village to another, very difficult. For the most part, they remained in their own villages and hamlets to defend them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From an organisational point of view, then, what was done in order to establish this army finally?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in order to finally establish this army, in my opinion, the idea of setting up a classical Viteska Brigade was abandoned, I mean one that would be in line with books of establishment and formation. According to orders issued by the Operative Command, sectoral defence was organised. That is to say that there weren't units within the brigade; there was a defence of sectors. That meant establishing defence according to sectors within the municipality -- of course, those parts that are under our control, naturally -- and then it would be easier to integrate that into a defence system. While one could not fully order such areas, but at least one could keep it under one's control to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this organisation involve the idea that you mentioned earlier on, that a soldier should be at home in his own village? Is that the underlying idea, the core of this idea?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the moment when the conflict broke out, could the brigade order the village guards -- oh, I do apologise. Let me put an introductory question in order to avoid any objection. What were village guards?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, village guards were -- how should I put this? -- some kind of arbitrary forms of organisation of persons in villages, in the sense of controlling the passage of foreign persons going through that area. Because when there is a war, there is usually crime and other undesired things, so people would guard their houses, their villages, especially during the night. I don't know. They would have a rifle or two, mostly old ones, but they would control passage through their villages, passage of strangers. So that's what it all boiled down to. During the day they weren't around really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not go into too many details. Just give me a "yes" or "no" answer. Did these village guards already exist in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, was there a diversity in the sense of were they joined, consisting of members of both ethnic groups in some villages, and in other villages not, and was it all subject to the situation as it was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third reason why I'm putting this question to you is: Did the brigade, when the conflict broke out, could it command village guards in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with the shift to the sector organisation, could then the brigade, even if indirectly, abolish or rather co-opt the village guards?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indirectly, no, because people realised that it was not a game anymore, that a real war had begun, and they began then to listen to what they were being said [as interpreted]. I don't know if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that when the conflict broke out, or rather, more specifically, as of the change to the sectoral system of organisation, the village guards ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village guards ceased to exist because the defence lines were established and there was no need to have those village guards in villages themselves, because now -- because at that time we were simply surrounded, and within that circle we were controlling our villages. So that there was no need for those village guards to exist any longer. They were incorporated in the defence, naturally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that the majority of those people, that is, the villagers of those villages, were called up?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No. No. I can say not through the conventional system of mobilisation, but men simply joined their neighbours, in that sense. But yes, one could call it mobilisation, because they were on defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I should now like to show a map which the witness drew, and which you reconstructed these sectors, on which he will indicate the structures of the defence, that is, how the defence was organised per sector in Vitez at the time, after we have produced the document. [In English] Your Honour, we will certainly tomorrow have the translation of those couple of remarks on the map. As I said, the witness prepared that when he came in The Hague two days ago. And I will now present also the document --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map will be number D86/2; and the next exhibit, D87/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Sajevic, will you please look at this document and tell us if you saw it before.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention to two things in this document and then we shall move on to the map. First tell us: Is there any doubt that this document was the document which the brigade sent to the Operative Zone, that is, to the Superior Command, with the signature of its Commander?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no doubt this was a document addressed to the Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The date of this document is the 24th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention to the first sentence in the document.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does transpire from this document, in point of fact?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It transpires from this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive my interrupting. We don't know the circumstances in which the witness saw this document before. It's not addressed to him. He's not in any sense, I think, an author of it. And what we are achieving in this way is, clearly, to have the words of the author laid before the Court. I'm not necessarily objecting to that, but I think more foundation should be laid before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You mean the author is Mr. Cerkez, who will be the appropriate person to introduce it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- technical points. I think that, at the very least, rather more foundation should be laid before the Chamber is invited by the Defence to allow such evidence to come in in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You can ask the witness, establish if you can, with the witness, whether he's any connection with this document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Sajevic, you heard the question. Did you take part in preparing the document? That is the first question. Did you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that you also saw this document at the time when it was produced?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that it was signed by Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that it was sent to the Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add that personally we got the -- the Defence got the copy of this document from the Blaskic case at that time. That was the only available copy we could get because brigade archives were not available during our preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, will you please explain to us this first sentence after we clarify those points.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first sentence in the text, we wrote it because on that same day, we had received from the Operative Zone, that is, the military district, we had received a document prompting us, egging us on to hurry up with the sectoral organisation of defence and according to their document, I don't remember of which date, we had done that. But apparently they did not get this document, I don't know why. So they were telling us to speed it up, to do it, and then we wrote this document the same day and sent it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second sentence, it also transpires from it -- what transpires from the second sentence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the second sentence, it proves that it transpires, that it was only as late as the 21st of April that we received the order from the Commander of the Operative Zone about the organisation of different sectors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only as late as the 21st of April, thank you. So does that mean and, I ask you to draw on your memory, not only the document, that it was only as late as the 21st of April that you changed over to this sector organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this sectoral organisation, could you -- what was the -- how much time did you need to do that; within hours, within days? How long did this process take to change over to this method of organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, the planning in the Command itself did not take much. But then its implementation on the ground, yes, it was a matter of days, perhaps as many as 15 or 20 days. As a matter of fact, those problems with the sectoral organisation, those problems that troubled us until the end of the war. But a great deal was done in the following 15, 20 days, perhaps a month. I can't really remember. It doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now look at the map, will you take the pointer, please, and with this document which specifies the defence sectors, I think on the pages that follow in the document, will you please now show to us where is which sector and explain it to us. What are the blue lines?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like this: The blue lines are the positions of our formations, if I may call them that. Here where it says the first sector, that means these two blue lines which are not connected, they are disconnected here because the UN forces were here in this place so that there were no positions there. And later on, logically, there were no conflicts there. The second sector or sector two, here, you can see it. The third sector. Now, I am not talking per feature on the ground from where to where, because one can find it in the report, but I can explain it if need be. And the fourth and the fifth sector. So we had five defence sectors, and every one of them was then subdivided into two or three defence areas. So those were smaller entities, smaller wholes within sectors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the green line represents what?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The green line represents the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when we liken it to the previous map, I see that there is a -- that this blue circle, in Croatian, it says "missing here. "

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was your group in Kruscica, wasn't it? Where is it now?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It pulled out because they were attacked at this facility, and this facility was demolished, I think, at that time. So they pulled out through the woods. They even took some civilians, Croats, who happened to be in Kruscica, and they took them along and went I don't know through where, but eventually they ended up in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Sajevic, when we had these sectors divided like this, at that time, that is during the first two days of the conflict, did the BH army attack Poculica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the BH army attacked Poculica right away on the 16th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grbavica, yes, but I don't know exactly when. Grbavica, I don't know whether it was on the 16th. I know about Poculica, but Grbavica, I don't know. But if it wasn't on the 16th it was on the 17th or what do I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the army attack Sivrino Selo or rather the hamlet called Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Krivaca on the first day of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krivaca, you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the lower part of Sivrino Selo. You can show us on the map where it is.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean Pirici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pirici, Vidovici, I think it's a mistake on the map. I think that should be switched. They switched their places. Let me ask you like this: Here is Sivrino Selo which is the right, lower part of Sivrino Selo but it says Pirici. That is Vidovici. And that part was attacked on the 16th of April, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Stari Vitez, the old part of the town, was completely closed and placed under the TO control, is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Let's not go into any further particulars, but I should merely like to ask you to explain to the Court the title of the map which you wrote, and it says that these are the defence sectors of parts of the Vitez Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us, you explained that this map reflects what transpires from this document.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, should I remove the maps from ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and tomorrow, make sure that the -- there are translations for these various statements on the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We will certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sajevic, in those early days of the conflict, it was heard, among other things, but I would like to focus on the following: Some events regarding Gacice, involving Gacice, and I would like to produce a map, sir, and the witness might show us some things that were mentioned on earlier occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we -- it was the Prosecution which was kind enough to supply us with this map, but it was never adduced into evidence and we were simply offered to use it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map will be marked Exhibit D88/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Sajevic, will you please show us here the following. The town of Vitez itself. To begin with, the town itself.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, very good. Secondly, the compound of the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you perhaps know how many hectares the SPS had?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it wasn't larger than the town, but they are roughly about the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever had an opportunity to see the area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But wouldn't you say that the town and the compound, it's SPS compound covered approximately the same area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that the SPS, yes, did, indeed, did take quite a lot of ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where does the SPS end because up there, I think there are some warehouses. Where does the SPS begin?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, no, to the left. To the left. You just passed it. To the left of your pointer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, these are the boundaries. So Witness Sajevic, tell us, please, villages are along the flanks of the SPS?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the SPS is flanked by Donja Veceriska and Gacice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us, please, just in military terms, can one control the SPS unless he also controls the Donja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so because both Donja Veceriska and Gacice are on elevations. They are elevated features as against a feature of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the same hold true of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So both those villages are not -- are higher, at a higher altitude than the SPS?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, it may be convenient time or I should continue and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a convenient time. We'll adjourn now. We're taking rather longer for the luncheon adjournment. We shall sit again at 3.00 and go on until half past 4.00 by which time I hope you're through this witness, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I sincerely hope, Your Honour, that I will be finished in that frame which you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Sajevic, we have now shown the position of Gacice and Donja Veceriska vis-à-vis the SPS. I do apologise if I'm repeating things, but you said that as far as altitude is concerned, both villages are above the SPS.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the town of Vitez, the approach to Gacice -- actually, Gacice is hardly accessible for an army that would try to reach Gacice from Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, since it is high up, it is in a better position than perhaps those who would be approaching Gacice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Gacice, at the time of the outbreak of the conflict, was there any military force there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Gacice it was mainly Bosniaks who lived there, so it was logical that the members of the BH army -- it is logical to expect that perhaps some of them lived there, and then maybe there were others from other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was your assessment?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that prove to be true later, that there indeed was a smaller unit up there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO took Gacice the next day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can say it was the HVO. I know that Gacice was an interesting feature because of the vicinity of Princip. However, at that time the Viteska Brigade did not have enough people in order to take every piece of territory that was of interest at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead. Does that mean that the brigade did not take Gacice?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Parts of the HVO Viteska Brigade did not take part in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which unit did take Gacice?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Gacice was taken by the so-called members of the special purposes unit of Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That unit was not under the command of the brigade, or of Commander Mario Cerkez, rather?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a so-called PPN unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said so just now. It was a PPN, Postrojba Posebne Namjere, a special purposes unit. That's just what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document now, and would you please take a look at it and confirm whether you know about this. The document is a report of the PPN Vitezovi. Please take a look at page 1. The rest is irrelevant at this point in time. Please look at page 1. Look at the sequence of events and places, and could you please comment upon the contents. In terms of the time and places mentioned, does this correspond to your memories and to the information you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Kovacic. The same points have to arise in relation to this report as have arisen in relation to earlier documents. Some foundation, it might be thought, should be laid before the witness comments on it, a matter for the Court. But I know nothing about this document myself at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear about it. Where does it come from and what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] It comes from my investigative work in Vitez during 1998. And if I may add, Your Honour, there were many documents, particularly in the last couple of weeks, which were introduced by the other side which we also have never seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That doesn't matter. It's your documents we're dealing with now. Ask the witness about this to see whether there's any foundation that can be laid for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The PPN Vitezovi, was it active in 1993 in the territory of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their existence was certainly known?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about them having written reports about their activities to their superiors or did you see anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see anything of that kind, because I had no insight into their work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it reasonable to expect that they, as a PPN, a special purposes unit, would write reports to their superior command?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. It is only logical. They would have had to report to someone, but I don't know who and to what extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, this report -- well, about it, can you first specify what is to be understood under PPN or PN? Secondly, it is signed, indeed, but we don't know who it is being sent to, so you might want to give us some specificity so as to assess this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I think I have the original here. At the end of the document there is a stamp, very clearly, and it says "PPN Vitezovi." And the signature here can be identified as the signature of Darko Kraljevic, the Commander of this unit, about which I believe we have heard quite a bit. In addition to that, there is yet another report of this unit that was exhibited during this trial. I don't have the number right now, but it was signed by the Deputy Commander, Dragan Vinac. Dragan Vinac was the deputy of Darko Kraljevic, according to the establishment. If there is any question regarding the authenticity of the document, I can bring a witness who can identify the signature. This is a purely technical matter. But with your permission, just a word or two more. The witness was there during these events, and my intention was to discuss the contents of the first few days, the first few critical days, mentioned on page 1, where all these places are mentioned. And we also have corroboration of this from the other evidence we have heard so far, and it is obvious that this shows -- I do apologise. I just want to see whether the witness believes that this information about Gacice -- that is, the first, second, third paragraph -- whether that is what we have been saying just now. The Vitezovi themselves say here that they took Gacice, and that is what the witness said as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but this witness can't produce this document. He can merely look at it and see what it says. We can see that on the 18th of April. Yes. However, a great many reports have been admitted in this case and I don't see why this one should be treated any differently. For the moment we'll admit it, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us confirm this. Let us go back to the mentioned paragraph. Witness Sajevic, paragraph 1, 2, 3. Paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain something to me. Is it correct that Darko Kraljevic used this action to humiliate you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could say so. I don't think that this was his ultimate objective, but he did take advantage of this. So at least verbally, he diminished the importance of the members of the Viteska Brigade, he glorified his own men as if they were the best in the world, that they could do anything and we were old women, it would have been better for us to have stayed at home, something of that sense. Well, I'm not trying to say that he did this only to diminish our importance, there were probably other reasons, but he did take advantage of this in order to devalue us in a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Sajevic, this assessment of his, regardless of the motives, were Kraljevic's Vitezovi a serious unit in comparison with the brigade, at least at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. If we take 30 men from the Vitezovi, for example, perhaps you could find a corresponding 30 men in the Viteska Brigade in terms of quality, but not more than that. I'm trying to say that if you would look at the same number of people, he had in a way more able, better men. Well, we could not have had 500 such men for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question related to Vitezovi. At the time when the war broke out, they already had certain experience and a well-established unit, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They certainly had experience, combat experience, and whether they had an established unit that, I don't know, because I don't really know whether they had an establishment. I don't know how they were set up, actually, on what basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. We've already addressed the topic that follows through the maps which explained your positions on the 16th of April. At that time, that is, you were not there for the first two days, but on the third day, when you did come up, come and collect the information, did you know then whose army was in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with accuracy when it was that I learned about Ahmici at all and the crime committed there. Whether it was on the third, fourth, on the fifth day, I really cannot say. But I know that shortly after I returned to the command, I heard about that and on one occasion, of obeying Mr. Cerkez's orders, I was visiting a part of the front line held by the Vitez Brigade. And the driver who took me along part of the road told me how all sorts of things happened in Ahmici and so on and so forth. It was from that day that I began to learn about this. Needless to say, I have been receiving more and more information about this to this day. Few people were willing to talk about it, at least of those who participated in that, as far as I know. But some specific reports or something in writing, I never had it in my hands. So that basically, I do know now what happened there and how it happened, and I also think that I know, after all, which parts of what units took part in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the purpose of this case, I should like to ask you to confirm whether this information that you gained in the days, in the wake of Ahmici, also included the effect that there were Jokers in Ahmici and a part of the active part of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what is more important is do you think -- do you think or is it true that Mario Cerkez, the Commander of the Vitez Brigade, from his superior, Tihomir Blaskic, never received any order regarding the action in Ahmici which took place on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- could it be possible that Cerkez issued such an order to his unit or anybody else without having received such orders from Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. I mean I was not there all the time so perhaps I wouldn't have known it on that particular day, but I would have learned about that during the war and later. I do not think there is any room for such theories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Vitez Brigade only later on the 7th of May, if I am correct, took the positions above Ahmici at the Krtine-Pirici, line?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, because in the early days of May, I think an order arrived from the military district that the Vitez Brigade should prepare a shift in order to replace some parts of the 4th Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] We were informed earlier that there are discoveries in Zagreb. We are indeed receiving, and we are cooperating with the Prosecution on that matter in order to try to avoid the problems of parallel discovery. Amongst other things, we agree that the party who will be able to produce translations of those documents first will exchange them with the other party. There is even a written agreement. However, I expected to have the translation of the very important document for our case this morning. Unfortunately, it did not come. I did give the copies to the booth, and I would suggest to read the documents which will be introduced to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long is this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We want a translation tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the practical purposes, if you oblige me to do that, I'm simply not sure I can oblige for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When are you going to do it by?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Give me at least two or three days. I guess that there is quite a good chance that the Prosecution will receive their translation also today, tomorrow. We are just trying to find that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. And Your Honour, if I may tell in advance, there is a similar document connected to that also very short with -- dated a little bit after that. It is not -- Your Honour, I think it is an interest of justice. This is the only witness which can confirm or deny such a documents. He was there. He was in operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's the point. And we didn't have that discovery on time. I would like to have usher, could you assist me? [Interpretation] I should like to remind the interpreters that they were given the copies of this document this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D90/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will read the main parts and short explanation just for the matter of translation, if that is expected of me. The document is by the header, it is issued by HVO. [Interpretation] This was issued by the HVO, the Commander of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia. It has its reference number. It was issued on the 7th of May 1993 at 11.45. The document is addressed to the attention of the Commander of the Vitez Brigade, and below that, in the second line, it says, "Commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police in Vitez." Notification, it says, in the brackets. The document is signed by Commander Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, his signature and seal. The subject matter of the document is "Zamjena VP na crti obrans" which means "exchange of military police on the defence line" below it "order". Then the first line, "In the light of the apparent need to engage the military police on police missions in the area of responsibility of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, I order, item one, without delay to embark on the preparations and ensure the replacement of members of the military police on the Krtine-Pirici defence line. Two, to effect the replacement on the 8th of May 1993 not later than 1200 hours and submit report to me on the performance of the task, on the performed task. Item three, the brigade commander will account to me for the compliance for the execution of this order." Then on the left-hand side, we see that it was typed in three copies and who the copies were sent to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question to the witness is: Would this document tell what you told us, that it was only in early May that you replaced the military police on the positions above Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this locality, Krtine-Pirici, where is it exactly? Can you describe it without having to resort to the map again?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is north-west of Ahmici but not far from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I get a number for the document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number given was D90/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we could skip item 7 of the events on the 20th of October, 1992, army of BH, but I should like to go back, in the briefest possible way, to this account, because we've heard a great deal about it so far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, we are talking about the events on the 20th of October, 1992. Again, these events largely took place on the road below Ahmici. Tell us, please: Do you know -- are you aware that on the 19th of October two checkpoints were raised in the same area, in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that one was at Bila, near the Bosna construction company?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you just answer me with "yes" or "no," to cut the time shorter. Are you aware that the checkpoint at the Bosna company, Mr. Franjo Nakic managed to remove through negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the BH army put up those checkpoints in order to prevent the departure of the HVO unit from Kiseljak and Busovaca in the direction of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 19th and the night between the 19th and the 20th, there were several rounds of negotiations between the civilian authorities of the HVO and the army of the HVO, that is, all the factors, in order to try to resolve it peacefully and to remove them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there were attempts at a peaceful solution of the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that at the end of the story, it was the Kiseljak forces which attacked the checkpoint and removed the barricade from the road?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was those forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that an HVO soldier from Kiseljak was killed there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that a soldier was -- a soldier from Kiseljak was killed and also a soldier from the BH army; if not a local man, then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That other one was a local man, but do you know if he was a Bosniak, was he a soldier, was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak and a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what you know about him? That's what you heard about this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have any particulars about this whole thing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, is it correct that during the attack on this roadblock on the road, several houses, several residential houses and some buildings were set on fire in the course of that action?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I don't remember, but I think -- I think that there were a couple of instances, but I can't really confirm that 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you quite positive that no serious damage was done?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about the fact that people were even compensated for those damages by the municipality to repair those houses?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as concerns your brigade, and that is why we are addressing this topic, this is the time when you still exist as the Municipal Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time did you undertake anything in order to organise your storage, the storage that came from Lovac and Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I remember now when this roadblock was put on the road. Since in Kruscica we had our depot of the materiel, of ammunition, and I don't know what else, and we then decided, I believe it was in the evening of the 19th, to get it out from Kruscica, because we were afraid that they might erect another barricade towards Kruscica and thus cut off this depot from us. Yes, that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that step simply in order to protect your depot of the materiel?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last question: Did the brigade have any military role in the attack on this roadblock and the dismantlement of the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you're asking me if soldiers, say, of our brigade, of the Vitez Brigade, participated in the attack on the roadblock. Is that what you meant, roughly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I wasn't precise enough. I meant the Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, right, Municipal Staff, because one cannot speak of the brigade, especially in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, members of those groups that we had did not directly participate in the removal of that roadblock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the materiel that you mentioned, did you manage to pull it out and store it safely?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next subject. Did you know a person called Marko Lujic, called Markesa, and some people called him gunman?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he ever an officer of the Vitez Brigade?
