utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he ever a member of the Command of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the officer responsible for artillery in the brigade, as of its inception?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Blazen Koramjak, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Blazen Koramjak, is he also mentioned in the document that we saw this morning, when the municipality issues its consent to the command?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are sure that Blazen Koramjak, as referred to in that document, was the officer responsible for artillery at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the brigade perhaps have a special post of a deputy or a chief for rocket systems?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Vitez Brigade have any rocket systems?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether this Marko Lujic whom we mentioned was head of war production in SPS?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Superficially or well?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very superficially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I do apologise. I have to lay the foundation for this. Practically throughout this period that we have been discussing, from 1990 onwards, you knew Cerkez, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise. Throughout this period you knew Cerkez, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously you spent quite a bit of time with him.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean at work, in the war, we spent quite a bit of time together. But if you're talking about the pre-war period, then no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. During the war and in relation to work.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in relation to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period of time that we are talking about, throughout the war, in the time when your only enemy was the Serb army, and later, when there was a conflict between the HVO and the BH army, did you ever, at any moment, hear Cerkez speak to the Muslims, as a people, in a derogatory or insulting manner?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember him ever having mentioned a derogatory word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. No. He did not usually speak in derogatory terms about anyone. Perhaps only about some individuals, extreme ones at that, but as a rule he would not speak in derogatory terms about the other side, regardless of whether it was the army or the Serb aggressor, et cetera. I think that he simply looked at this as a soldier. He simply saw the enemy as the enemy, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an HVO officer, did you ever, from any order, written or oral, those sent from your command to others or from superior commands, did you ever see that the -- anything that would show that the HVO wished to pursue a policy of persecution of Muslim civilians in your area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, bearing in mind all the events that you were involved in, what was the main objective of the BH army in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, one of the main objectives of the BH army in the Lasva Valley was to take the area of special purpose production in Vitez, which could logically be explained by the fact that they already had in their hands Bratstvo in Novi Travnik, that is to say, a factory of weapons; they had Slavko Rodic in Bugojno, a factory for equipment, for explosive devices. So obviously they needed an explosives factory. Any army would want that, to have ammunitions and weapons manufactured in their own hands. They had Konjic in their hands as well, so they needed this to round off this process of production. I think that this was one of the basic objectives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To finish on this note, until the Washington Accords and until the ceasefire, the main lines of attack went in which direction?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions this was confirmed, viewing the movements in the Lasva River Valley. At any rate, they wanted to use a classical manner of waging war, to cut up this valley so that it would be easier for them to take other parts of the valley in this way. As for Vitez, the main directions of attack were going towards Princip, from the south and from the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Your Honour, maybe it's an opportunity just to break. We just got the translation, and that is the result of Prosecution efforts through the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I interject to say one thing. It may be at some stage the Chamber will be helped by being informed in a little more detail of the difficulties of the translation of these documents and the protocol that's observed by the Unit. Nevertheless, I have been able to provide a draft translation, I hope of both documents that Mr. Kovacic wants. And we'll have to await the full translation in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is the translation of one which is already tendered. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, at any time during 1993, and even during 1992, to be realistic, but at any time, the Commander of Viteska Brigade, Mario Cerkez, could he command Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could he have commanded any other special purposes unit of the HVO that was temporarily or permanently stationed in the territory of the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Cerkez ever command any units outside the municipality of Vitez except at Kalina, Slatka Vode, and elsewhere where you fought against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not. None of those units, except when he was in Tomasevic. So part of the forces from Novi Travnik, but that was while it was a joint brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean while you were fighting against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the military concept you had, in which case could Cerkez command any other HVO unit or any special purposes unit under those circumstances, hypothetically speaking? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, hypothetically speaking, he could have commanded, for example, if the Command of the military district was not in Vitez, that is to say, if our Superior Command had not been there. Automatically, Mr. Cerkez could not command units in the same locality where the Command of the military district is, that is to say, where the Commander of the military district is and where he is of course the superior officer. So had he been in some other area where the highest command was the Brigade Command, then he could have commanded attached units, depending on the orders that he would receive, in terms of time and place, and also for that period of time for which this unit would be attached to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean only as defined by such an order?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, a higher command was also mentioned here. The Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. How far away from them were you, 200 metres, 300 metres? Tell us, what do you think?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, about 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the hotel to the cinema?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, maybe it's 40 metres. I really don't know. I never measured it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it sometimes difficult during the war to get from one of those buildings to the other one?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I add something? It was difficult to get from one building to another because there was a sniper that was operating from Mahalla all the time. It's a straight street, and you could see it very well. And we would run across from one to another during the day but during the night, one could pass from one building to the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point in time, did Blaskic actually ask Cerkez to try to take Gacice? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure, but I think -- well, he probably did ask, because Mr. Cerkez explained that we did not have the forces needed for such an action so to speak. So I imagine this was asked, but I did not see a written order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you only know that Cerkez was explained that he could not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that basis, you assumed that that is what he was asked?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is actually linked to this story that Kraljevic took advantage of this to humiliate you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, you knew Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were actually present when he was brought in on the evening of the 19th of April to the premises of Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present. But if we could -- if we say that he was brought in, perhaps one could assume that this was done by force but, no, he came of his own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what capacity did he come?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muhamed Mujezinovic, a physician, is one of the renowned citizens of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major Sajevic, you needn't go through this. Now, just tell us what happened that evening. What is the point that you wanted to get at, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What the witness told me, the story was not entirely as Dr. Mujezinovic witnessed, and I would like to clear up at least some basic details on that event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, but do so quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if you remember, Your Honour, we did challenge at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any rate, Dr. Mujezinovic held a position within the party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which post he held in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was one of the leaders of the party, that, you do know, right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were already mentioned why he was invited to come so we will skip that now. Do you remember that a day before that event, a day before Mujezinovic came, because he was asked to come under escort, that there was a ceasefire signed at a higher level; Izetbegovic, Boban?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there was some kind of a ceasefire that had allegedly been signed, but there had been such ceasefires during the war too and they were not observed. But yes, some kind of an agreement was signed. I don't know what they called it, a ceasefire or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the situation in town, would it have been safe for Dr. Mujezinovic to go from his house to the command by himself?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mujezinovic came, a meeting was held, right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some other persons joined in who had been detained in the cinema, persons who were ethnic Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the -- what was the subject of that meeting, can you explain this in a few words?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think this was Mr. Cerkez's idea that we invite the more prominent citizens of Vitez and that they address, through TV Vitez, all the citizens of Vitez, notably those of Muslim descent to stop some of the rumours that were going around, inter alia, that Dr. Mujezinovic had been killed while he was doing his job, as always, at the medical centre. And, how should I put this, to influence the Bosniak part of the population of Vitez so that things would calm down and so that this could some how be put under control. Everything seemed to be getting out of control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness Sajevic, do you remember Cerkez attended the meeting, did he leave before you or after you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez left before I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were there at the meeting all the time while Cerkez was there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in time, while Cerkez was there, did he, in any way, directly or indirectly threaten Mujezinovic or anyone else at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No way. Actually, Mr. Cerkez besieged these people. That is what he said, "Please, go and speak to these people on television. Don't let people mistreat you." And Dr. Mujezinovic had not been interned at any point, and he was asking these people kindly. He was besieging them literally, so that everybody could see that Mujezinovic had not been killed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had just mentioned the Vitez television. The Vitez television was in the same building as you were in; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their premises were, I think, on the other side of the corridor on the same floor where you were.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the same hall. And not only the television, I think that the HDZ premises were there as well. I don't know. I think that Radio Vitez also it's had its premises there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Never mind that now. During this meeting and conversation, especially Cerkez while he was there, did anyone say to Dr. Mujezinovic that the HVO held 2.323 detainees, and did anybody threaten that these people would be killed if the attack was not stopped?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. No way. This is outlandish. No one made any threats. No one mentioned any number of detained persons or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody at this meeting, especially Cerkez, mention the events of Ahmici as an implied threat?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear that. I was present all the time, but I did not hear that from anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that moment, could Cerkez have known how many persons there were interned in Vitez in the territory of the entire municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Perhaps he could have known but he didn't have to know. But I doubt that he could have known because this situation changed practically from one hour to another. And perhaps we don't even know the exact number until the present day. We don't have exact information.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the third day of the conflict around 1900 hours in the evening, I know you can't say exactly how many persons there were, but how many persons, how many men, ethnic Muslims could have been detained in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It is hard to tell. I think it could have been around 200. Perhaps I'm making a mistake by 10 or 20 or 30. I don't know. I really can't tell. There were cases that people were brought in, and then we would let sick people leave or would take them to the hospital, and people would come of their own free will. They would say that they didn't dare stay at home, at their own homes, and they came there for their own protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, could you slow down for the interpreters, please, and leave a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, the figure of 200, is that the highest number that ever was in the cinema according to you, bearing in mind all the possible variations, or do you think that that particular day, that was the highest number of people?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the largest number of people ever reached but that is my opinion. I cannot really say whether that was so or not, but I do think that that was the largest number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you told us already some particulars about the internees but since you shared the building, you, the television and the internees, who -- under whose control were the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under the military police control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military police had brought them to the cinema; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military police was downstairs on the ground floor and controlled the building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The 4th Battalion of the Military Police had its command where?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Military Police 4th Battalion was also housed in the hotel together with the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In contrast with, for instance, the brigade, the members of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police had their own base. They slept, that is, they had -- they were there around the clock?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they slept in the hotel. That is in the rooms of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on, is it true that they came by another building which was opposite your warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Later on they had another building, the building which now houses the first basic court in Vitez and they used the building for their purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that sense, they were an army with a barracks?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me rephrase this. You had, in the building, and around the building, you had a platoon and everybody called it the brigade military police, will you please tell us who was that, what was it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we all called them the brigade military police, but it wasn't on the basis of any particular organisation or even the documents on the establishment of the brigade. The brigade did not have such information. It was some of the military police of the 4th Battalion who were standing guard around the command of the military district, and since the command of the brigade was in the immediate vicinity, then they simply provided security for both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was the platoon which was in your building?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, to try to be quite clear so that everybody can understand, in colloquial, in your vernacular, in the idiom that you used, what did you call them the military police or the brigade or what did you say? How did you call them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was easy to call the brigade military police rather than 1st, 2nd or I don't know, the 3rd platoon or the 4th Battalion of the Military Police. So we simply called it the brigade military police, the brigade MP because, in a manner of speaking, some of them had been assigned to the Vitez Brigade for assistance and what -- what do I know, to perform a role of the military police because the brigade did not have a military police of its own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, did ever any officer from the brigade command or perhaps the Commander Cerkez -- could directly issue orders to that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you needed this brigade MP to bring in a soldier or something, how did you go about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would submit a written request to the Commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police or would seek, through the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, to authorise the use of military police in that area or -- I think we were very specific about this, and asked them to authorise us to ask the military police to bring in so and so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military police had held the lobby in your building; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the brigade police stood guard around your building?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if a party came, if a visitor came and had to go to the first floor, then who checked his ID, who searched him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they, again, but I have to say, I am using the term brigade military police conditionally. They were members of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police. So again, they did not belong to the brigade but we keep calling them the brigade military police. So that was the common term. Everybody called them that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I guess that they, themselves, used this, I mean because they had to know who was in the Operative Zone, who was working for the brigade because sometimes they would dispatch some men to the other brigades, not only the Vitez one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us, please, this impossibility to issue them orders, the fact that your command could not issue orders to those men who were in your building, it also gave rise to a certain personnel problems, didn't it, who was superior to whom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could any officer, either by placing that request or by issuing a direct order make those members of the brigade MP to go, to issue them any combat order or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or to go into the town and arrest somebody?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you. If we needed, say, some services, some of the services of those military policemen, then we wrote requests to their commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, sorry, I apologise. And finally, do you remember when did this chain of command change?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That chain of command changed, if I remember well, in the summer of 1993, that is, there were already so many misunderstandings regarding the subordination of the military police because, of course, the brigade commander also wanted to have a couple of MPs who he could issue orders to. And he didn't have any, because those military policemen were all members of the 4th Battalion the Military Police, and they considered they were higher-ranking soldiers than all the other soldiers. So there were certain arguments from time to time, and I think that in August or perhaps late July, I can't be quite exact, an order arrived whereby parts of the military police assigned to the brigades would be placed under the command of brigade commanders. That is as of that moment, brigade commanders could issue direct orders to those military policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We obtained those documents at five minutes to 12.00, so will you please look at these documents and tell us if that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is the one, Your Honour, I said that there is no translation, but there is now a translation thanks to my dear colleague. Could we get a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Shall I say, Mr. Kovacic, long live such cooperation with your dear colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I appreciate that really very much, and we will also exchange the lists of the documents which we received from Zagreb because there seems to be also some administrative problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sajevic, you have in front of you the -- a document of -- dated 18th of August, 1993. Could you tell us if that is the document that you mentioned and which now makes quite clear what are the relations and which places the police under the brigade command, that is, this one unit which was called, in your vernacular, the brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document which even makes a step forward, further, and enables the brigade commander to even replenish the military police, that is, to bring in the new man to replenish the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, according to the army doctrine, could one say that this document enables the Vitez Brigade Commander to indeed exercise all the commanding powers over not only his brigade, but including that unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Your Honours, I will try to buy some time just briefly going through the next point, 15, since I think we, in the meantime, had another witness on the issue. But just briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sajevic, we also talked in Vitez before we came here, and we showed you a long list, the 1779 post code, the three large sheets.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the list of personnel?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the Vitez Brigade, at its peak in late 1993 -- it's impossible to reconstruct that -- numbered 1.800 men?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can concur with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does anybody know to what size the Vitez Brigade rose at its peak?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if anybody knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody operate with any figures in that regard, publicly?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, because I left the army in 1995, so now I cannot recall. And probably those who worked in personnel have such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with a very general assessment -- and I don't know if you can agree with this or not -- that since some people came, some left, some were killed, some were wounded, that over 2.200 people came and went through this brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they could come and go. Whatever was the Vitez Brigade, that was it. I'm not saying that there were not members of other units who came to assist in certain specific situations, but that would be for brief periods of time and they would go back to their own units. One knew, if there was a need for the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade to help with 20 or 30 people for five, ten days, then they would send it. I don't know if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I had in mind is that some people were killed, so they're gone; then other people came.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people fluctuated, but I don't think that there could have been more than 2.200 people who were ever involved, who passed through that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will skip the area on the map. We agreed on everything except for a few details, the Elford map, and I believe that we covered all the topics. That is point 16. I would just like to ask the registry to please help us with another document. That would be D70/2, to put to this witness. This document was tendered through Witness Puljic a few days ago, and the witness mentioned it, so perhaps we can find it relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, would you please carefully look at the document. I only have two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen it in my office, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear from this document that this is a Defence Office -- issued by the Defence Office which you mentioned, which was organised as part of the HVO government in Vitez. Is that that institution?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is the Defence Office of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. So this is a higher level?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the higher level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Municipal Defence Office reports to this administration which is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it should be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any doubt that this is the civilian branch of government?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Mr. Pero Skopljak -- was Mr. Pero Skopljak a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this document corroborate your knowledge about the detention of people, their guarding and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, as it's stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You previously said that the military police guarded them. Was that just their -- it includes physical protection or does it refer to the essence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police guarded them while they were in the cinema, physically guarded them. I'm not sure that I understood your question fully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was whether the military police just carried out the physical aspects of detention, that is, guarding and so on, but in terms of the detention itself, that the civilian government was responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say so, because there were commissions for exchange at the Central Bosnia Operative Zone level. So I don't believe that this was a military police task. I think that there was a separate commission which was tasked with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can agree that the civilian authorities were in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Your Honour, I think I'm done with this witness. Just as a matter of courtesy, we did file an affidavit which, in some little parts, corroborate this testimony, and there is no need to explain that, I guess. If there is, I will be glad to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll use the usual procedure for the affidavits. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, allow me to introduce myself. I'm Mitko Naumovski, attorney from Zagreb, and alongside Mr. Browning, represent the Defence of Mr. Dario Kordic. I know that you have been questioned all day. You must be exhausted. I will try to be very brief. You are a soldier, you spent -- you were involved in military affairs for the most of your career. Let me ask you first off: What was Dario Kordic for you, a politician or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In short, to me, Mr. Dario Kordic was a politician. If I need to further elaborate, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I don't think we need to go any wider than that. Can you please tell us: Throughout the period when you were a member of the HVO staff in Vitez and later on a member of the Vitez Brigade Command staff, did Mr. Dario Kordic ever issue any military order at any time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me, and I don't know of any case when he issued any kind of military order to anyone in the Vitez Command, because we had our own Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little while ago, some civilians from the Vitez authorities were mentioned: Pero Skopljak, the HDZ president, and then a document signed by Anto Valenta, who was the vice-president of the civilian government. My question to you is: Did any of the civilians ever have any authority or issue any military orders to the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one ever did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me: Have you ever seen Mr. Kordic, or did Mr. Kordic ever visit your command post?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war I only saw Mr. Kordic once, which does not mean that he never came to the command post of the Vitez Brigade, but I wasn't there; I'm not aware of his having come. But I saw him in the command post of the 1st Battalion. I think that that was in early 1994 when he stopped by. He stayed there three to five minutes. He greeted everyone, he said, "How's everything," he said, "Hold on tight," and he went on another business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you haven't heard from anyone else that he was coming to your brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. Even if somebody had mentioned it to me, I didn't remember. And right now, I cannot recall him ever coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that throughout this period -- 1991, 1992, and 1993 -- you may have heard or been aware of some of his press conferences or his speeches during some celebrations. Have you ever heard Mr. Kordic speaking in negative terms against the Muslims or any other ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. And I heard him -- I listened to a number of Mr. Kordic's speeches. Mr. Kordic always underscored that the Croats should not leave the territory, that they should not leave this area, that this was also our country, not just of others. And I never heard him say anything derogatory about any other ethnic groups: Serbs or Muslims or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move to another topic. You mentioned a checkpoint, a blockade, at the Catholic cemetery near Ahmici. In late 1992, did you ever hear Mr. Kordic issuing any threats to the people in Ahmici if they did not remove the barricade which they had placed there in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard him issuing any threats to anyone, not only on that occasion, but ever. I think that Mr. Kordic was a politician of such a level that he wouldn't even contemplate such a thing. That's my perception, that it would have been below him to go and threaten people at barricades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned 15 April 1993 and the fact that you had a temperature, that you were sick on that day. Did you hear through the media, television or anywhere else, that Mr. Kordic on that day, 15 April 1993, said that the Croats were ready, that the Croatian units were ready, and that that would have been expressed as some kind of a threat, preparedness for some kind of an action?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, let me tell you: I don't believe so, because Mr. Kordic is a man of such a calibre that he must have known quite well the position of Croats in Central Bosnia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, rather than say something like that. Seventeen per cent of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot present such a force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you heard nothing of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An additional question regarding another subject matter. Mr. Sajevic, you would be the right person to ask such a question, because you were there all the time. Were there any units of the Croatian army in Central Bosnia, that is, in the area under control of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, not a single soldier, except perhaps for Croatia, Galic, who was a person from Vitez who had spent a period of time in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours. That concludes my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning, Mr. Nice. Do you anticipate being able to tailor your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's quite a problem, because the evidence, one way or another, covers the totality of the Cerkez defence. I've been thinking it over this afternoon. It seems to me inevitable that I won't be able to cover the whole of the Prosecution case against Mr. Cerkez, although the Rules might technically require me to do it, and I shall be selective, I think. Might it be helpful, because I know the translation problem is a problem, if I just explain to you, perhaps after the witness has gone, why things are difficult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think -- you needn't explain. I'm sure they are difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I fully sympathise with Mr. Kovacic's position and I understand the difficulties he's facing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Major Sajevic, would you be back, please, tomorrow morning, half past 9.00, to continue your evidence. We'll adjourn.
